name: Marco Patel

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Marco. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm on an overhead crew for the city power company, mostly the old east side where the poles are in the back lots behind the houses. We meet at the yard at seven, check the bucket truck, number 41, and get our jobs for the day. Half of it is climbing, because you can't get a truck into those back lots, so it's hooks and a belt like it's 1975. I love that part, honestly, it's quiet up there.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The storm call-outs. Last March I did nineteen hours straight after the ice, then slept four and went back. My girlfriend Priya is a nurse on nights, so some weeks we just pass each other in the kitchen. But the pay's good, and I've got close to ten months put away in the credit union, so I'm not complaining much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so. Everybody at the yard has a cousin who says robots are coming for us, and I'd just laugh. Nobody's sending a robot up a rotten pole behind Mrs. Kaur's garden.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, that's the world I expect. My job is wire, wood and weather, and AI doesn't change any of those. It means I keep doing what I do until my knees give out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing, really. I'd keep climbing, keep paying into the union, keep the savings where they are. Maybe I'd finally take the week off Priya's been asking for, because there'd be nothing to worry about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. Relaxed, even. It's the version where all the noise turns out to be noise.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there any part of your work where AI already shows up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The office has some new scheduling system that's supposed to be smart. It sends us to the wrong side of town half the time, so we call Denise in dispatch and she sorts it. I've never typed a word into one of those chat things and I don't plan to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about the older guys on the crew? Would this picture change anything for them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gus, who I eat lunch with, has thirty years in. He'd just carry on to his pension. For him this is the best news, he doesn't want anything new before he goes.

S0.say: He'd tell the yard he was right all along, that nobody sends a robot up a rotten pole in a back lot. He'd laugh off the cousins who warned about robots.
S0.think: He privately agrees with his public line: his work is wire, wood and weather, and he expects to keep doing it until his knees go. AI doesn't touch the hard parts of the job.
S0.do: Keeps climbing, keeps paying union dues and leaves his ten months of savings where they are. Might finally take the week off his girlfriend has been asking for.
S0.feel: Relaxed and a little vindicated. This is the world he already expects.
S0.quote: Nobody's sending a robot up a rotten pole behind Mrs. Kaur's garden.
S0.fieldNote: Marco's sense of safety comes from the physical job, especially the back-lot climbing that trucks can't reach. He has never used an AI tool and takes some pride in that. The bad scheduling system gives him a ready story about tech that doesn't work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the office people who should worry, not us. At work I'd probably be the guy saying we need the union on this early, before management buys some gadget and calls it progress. Online I don't post much, but I'd share the union's stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it'd be the paperwork and the planning that change, and I wouldn't miss either. The risk is they use it as a reason to cut crew sizes from four to three and call it efficient. That's the bit I don't trust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to every union meeting instead of every third one, and I'd push for a clause that crew sizes stay where they are, whatever tools come in. Money-wise I'd keep doing what I do. I'm not changing trades over some software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Not for me so much as for how the company would use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which tasks on your crew do you think would change first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably the inspection side. They already fly drones over the big lines. Next they'll want a camera telling us which pole to replace instead of a guy who's been looking at poles for ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said nothing changes for you, but you also brought up the union twice. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both, I guess. My hands are safe, but my crew isn't automatically safe, if that makes sense. The job stays, but they could squeeze it.

S1.say: He'd say office workers should worry more than lineworkers, but that the union needs to get ahead of management. He'd share union posts online rather than write his own.
S1.think: He expects AI to take paperwork and planning, which he wouldn't miss. His real fear is the company using it to cut crews from four to three.
S1.do: Starts going to every union meeting and pushes for a clause that keeps crew sizes fixed whatever tools come in. Keeps his money and trade exactly as they are.
S1.feel: Mildly uneasy, more about the company's motives than about his own skills.
S1.quote: My hands are safe, but my crew isn't automatically safe, if that makes sense.
S1.fieldNote: His worry here isn't the technology but what a cost-cutting employer would do with it. When I named the contradiction he separated his own job from the crew, which says a lot about how he sees the work. He would act through the union, not alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Publicly I'd say it's a stunt until I see it in an ice storm. But I'd also be saying, loud, that whoever owns these robots owes the rest of us. If a company replaces a whole crew, the money it saves shouldn't all go to shareholders.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, if a robot can really climb and splice and work live lines in two years, I'm in trouble. I've got no plan B. I left school at seventeen for this, and the only thing I know how to do is this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First thing, I'd stop the car fund and put every spare bit into savings, because ten months could need to last a lot longer. I'd go to the union hall and ask what they're doing, and if the answer is nothing, I'd help organise. I'd be writing to the city council too, since they own the company, about protecting the crews.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the floor tilting. I'd be up at night, I know I would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years isn't long. What does the next twelve months look like if you know this is coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years means there's no time to train for anything else properly, and I wouldn't even know what to train for, since the robots do that too. So I'd spend that time fighting for a deal: keep us on, or pay us properly to leave. That's all the time gets you.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Priya that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her I'm scared, which I don't say often. Then I'd probably say at least people will still need nurses, and she'd say don't count on it. That's how that conversation would go.

S2.say: He'd call it a stunt until he saw it work in an ice storm, while arguing loudly that whoever owns the robots owes the workers they replace. He'd say savings shouldn't all go to shareholders.
S2.think: He believes that if robots can really climb and work live lines in two years, he has no plan B. He left school at seventeen for this trade and knows nothing else.
S2.do: Stops his car fund and moves every spare amount into savings, then goes to the union hall and helps organise if nothing is happening. Writes to the city council, which owns the company, about protecting crews.
S2.feel: Scared and sleepless, a feeling like the floor tilting under him.
S2.quote: I left school at seventeen for this, and the only thing I know how to do is this.
S2.fieldNote: Two years strips away the safety he leaned on in the first two pictures. He sees no point retraining because he can't name a job the robots wouldn't also take, so he turns entirely to bargaining. The public city ownership of his employer matters to him as a lever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, but calmer. I'd say this is exactly when the government should step in, with real rules on how fast companies can replace people. I'd say it at the bar and I'd say it at union meetings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd still be thinking I've got no plan B, just a longer runway. Five years means I'm thirty-two when it lands, which feels better than twenty-nine. I'd have more saved, at least.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and keep saving, probably pushing to a year and a half of expenses. I'd get more involved in the union, maybe run for steward, since someone has to be in the room. Like I said with the fast one, I'm not going to learn a new trade that a robot also learns.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried but not frozen. It's a slow leak instead of a burst pipe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does having five years instead of two change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives the union time to win something, a retraining fund or a payout per year of service. It also gives politicians time to waste, so I wouldn't count on it. But it's enough time to try.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone at work you'd worry about more than yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our apprentice, Leon. He's twenty and just started. He'd be finishing his training right as it lands, which is brutal. I'd want the union to fight for him first.

S3.say: He'd argue in public and at union meetings that this is exactly when government should set real rules on how fast companies replace people. He'd say it calmly rather than in anger.
S3.think: He still feels he has no plan B, only a longer runway. Being thirty-two instead of twenty-nine when it arrives, with more saved, feels a little better.
S3.do: Keeps working and builds savings toward eighteen months of expenses. Gets more involved in the union and considers running for steward, while refusing to retrain into a trade robots will also learn.
S3.feel: Worried but not frozen, like a slow leak rather than a burst pipe.
S3.quote: It's a slow leak instead of a burst pipe.
S3.fieldNote: The extra three years lower his panic but don't change his strategy, which is all collective. His concern quickly moved to the twenty-year-old apprentice, which showed his loyalty to the crew. He is honest that politicians may waste the time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got no excuse. Ten years is long enough to plan properly, so if workers get dumped anyway, that's a choice somebody made. I'd say it to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years makes it feel less personal. I'd be thirty-seven, I'd have years of good pay saved, and Gus's generation would be retired. I still don't believe it'll happen, but if it does, I'd have time to get my head round it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd mostly keep going as I am. Union meetings, steward if they'll have me, and voting for whoever is serious about rules on automation. I'd keep saving like normal, I don't need to panic with ten years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, but it's far enough off that I'd sleep fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, would you think about a different line of work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Priya would say yes, obviously, train for something. Maybe, if the union got a course paid for. But I'll be honest, I'd probably drag my feet until it was right on top of me, that's how I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want the union or the government to do with that decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Make the companies pay into a fund for every job they cut, and let us vote on how it's used. A decade is plenty of time to set that up. If they can build a robot lineman, they can build that.

S4.say: He'd say a decade leaves no excuse, so if workers get dumped anyway it's a choice someone made. He'd say it to anyone who would listen.
S4.think: Ten years makes it feel less personal: he'd be thirty-seven with years of savings and the older crew retired. He still doubts it will happen but would have time to adjust.
S4.do: Keeps working as normal, stays active in the union and aims to become a steward. Votes for candidates serious about automation rules and saves at his usual rate.
S4.feel: A little uneasy, but the date feels far enough away that he'd sleep fine.
S4.quote: If they can build a robot lineman, they can build that.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade, Marco relaxes into his usual pattern of waiting and organising. He openly admits he would drag his feet on retraining, which fits his dislike of change. His demand is concrete: a fund paid per job cut, with workers voting on it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, easily. It's the only one where I've got no time to do anything but panic. What would help is the union already having a deal in a drawer, a payout and a guarantee that crews don't get cut overnight, so I'm not starting from zero.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask who gets the money. Everybody asks if the robot can do my job. Nobody asks who's richer the day after it does.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Thank you. That's everything I needed.

headlineQuote: Nobody asks who's richer the day after it does.
portrait: Marco Patel is a 27-year-old overhead lineworker for a city-owned power company, who still climbs poles in back lots that trucks can't reach. He lives with his girlfriend Priya, a night-shift nurse, has close to ten months saved and has never used an AI tool. In the milder pictures he feels safe because his work is physical, though he worries the company would use AI to shrink crews. The fast AGI picture scares him because he has no plan B, and his answer at every speed is the union and the city council rather than retraining. With ten years he admits he would mostly wait.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because two years leaves time only to panic and no trade to retrain into.
whatWouldHelp: He'd want the union to have a deal ready in advance, with a payout and a guarantee that crews aren't cut overnight.
